name: The Catalogue Column
symptom: A single column whose three parts come from three different pages. The commonest version: a plain parallel shaft, an Attic base (plinth, torus, scotia, torus) which belongs to Gibbs's Doric and the Ionic, and a Roman Doric or Scamozzi Ionic capital chosen from a photograph. Second version: a Corinthian capital of cast polyurethane on a shaft whose diameter was set by a Tuscan load table, so the capital's bell is visibly wider than the shaft can carry and the acanthus leaves sit on nothing. Third and worst: a capital and base of different MATERIALS and different weathering — a cast stone base, an FRP shaft, a polyurethane capital — assembled with visible sealant joints.

cause.explanation: Column manufacturers sell shafts, caps and bases as independently orderable line items, and the ordering screen encourages exactly this. A shaft is priced by diameter and height; a capital by style name; a base by diameter. Nothing in the ordering process asks whether the three belong to the same order, and the cheapest capital and base for any given diameter are usually from different orders because tooling amortisation differs. The specifier picks 'Roman Doric cap' because it looks right in the thumbnail and 'Attic base' because it is standard, and the shaft because it is what fits.
cause.cost_saved: Nothing consistent — a matched set typically costs the same as a mismatched one. Where it does save money it is 40-120 USD a column, by taking whatever capital is in stock rather than waiting six weeks for the correct one.

rule_violated.ref: georgian-colonial-american / column / base = attic base: plinth, lower torus, scotia between fillets, upper torus
rule_violated.statement: The base is named by the order and by the authority, and the choice is legible from the street.

Gibbs gives his Doric an Attic base — upper torus, scotia, under torus, plinth — where Vignola's Doric base is plinth, torus, astragal, apophyge. This is the commonest single difference between an English Georgian Doric column and an Italian one, and it is visible from across a street.
The Tuscan base is a plinth and a single torus with a fillet and apophyge. It has no scotia at all, so an Attic base under a Tuscan capital is a member that the order does not contain.

rule_violated.ref: a column is one member with three parts, not three members
rule_violated.statement: Base, shaft and capital sum to the column height by invariant in every pack. If they are chosen independently they cannot sum correctly, and the shaft absorbs the error.

correct_practice: Choose the order first, then take base, shaft and capital from that order and that authority together. The heights are invariant and checkable: in Vignola's Tuscan the base is 1 module (half a diameter), the capital 1 module, the shaft 12 modules, summing to 14; in the Ionic 1 + 16 1/3 + 1 = 18 by the engine's own invariant, with the capital measured to the top of the abacus list. Gibbs's Ionic gives a full capital of one module against Vignola's 3 5/16 in at the same diameter, which is a real published difference and not an artefact — so an authority must be named, not just an order. Where the shaft is a stock diameter, size the capital and base to THAT diameter from the same authority's table, and if the vendor does not make them, change the order to one the vendor does make.

fixes.right: Buy the column as a matched assembly from one manufacturer's one order, specified by authority where the vendor publishes one. Any vendor who cannot say which order and which authority a capital is drawn from is selling a shape.
fixes.cheap: Go Tuscan. The Tuscan has the fewest parts, the fewest ways to go wrong, is correct on the largest number of American styles, and is the cheapest capital and base in every catalogue. A correct Tuscan column at 7 diameters costs less than an incorrect Ionic one and is right on a farmhouse, a Georgian outbuilding, a Colonial Revival porch, a Shingle Style veranda and a Greek Revival side porch.
fixes.dishonest: Painting the whole assembly one colour so the material joints disappear. The joints are not the fault; the mismatched profiles are, and paint makes the profile mismatch MORE visible by removing the material distraction. Equally dishonest: a decorative collar or 'necking ring' applied at the shaft-to-capital joint to cover a diameter mismatch, which is a member no order contains.

detection: From a close photograph of one column, run three checks. (1) Base: count the mouldings between the plinth and the shaft. Two tori with a scotia between them is an Attic base and belongs to the Ionic, the Corinthian and Gibbs's Doric. One torus is Tuscan or Vignola's Doric. (2) Capital: no ornament, square abacus with an ovolo under it is Tuscan or Doric; volutes is Ionic; acanthus is Corinthian. (3) Compare the two answers. An Attic base under a Tuscan capital, or a single-torus base under a Corinthian capital, is this fault. Fourth check, which finds the cast-parts version instantly: measure the capital's bell diameter at its base against the shaft diameter at the neck. They should be equal — the capital grows out of the shaft. A visible step in either direction means the parts were sized independently.

test.note: The astragal at the neck is the only place base, shaft and capital have to agree geometrically, and it is the fastest photographic evidence that they came from different pages. This test catches the sizing mismatch; the order mismatch itself is a categorical check on base moulding count against capital type and cannot be reduced to a ratio.

severity_by_style.why: Jefferson specified order and authority by name and had capitals carved in Italy to plate. Mixed parts are a category error.

Benjamin's Grecian Doric is baseless — the shaft stands directly on the stylobate. An Attic base under a Greek Doric capital is not merely a mismatch but a contradiction of the order's defining feature.
The idiom is a catalogue assembly and always was; the mill sold parts and the carpenter combined them.

exceptions.why: The Folk Victorian porch IS a catalogue assembly and its history is the history of the Sears and Roebuck millwork page. Turned posts, sawn brackets and spindle friezes were bought as separate line items and combined by the local carpenter, and the combination is the style.
exceptions.bounds: Applies only to the turned-post and sawn-ornament vocabulary. The moment a moulded classical capital appears — Ionic volutes, acanthus, a Roman Doric abacus — the order has been invoked and the order's discipline applies.

exceptions.why: Shingle Style columns are deliberately reduced and hybridised: a plain torus base, no plinth, a shaft with no fluting and a capital that may be a simple moulded block. This is a considered primitivism reaching back past Vignola, not an assembly error.
exceptions.bounds: The reduction must be consistent and downward — a SIMPLER capital than the order requires, never a richer one. A Corinthian capital on a stout Shingle Style Tuscan shaft is this fault, not the exception.

exceptions.why: The style's whole method is the sawmill reinterpreting masonry Gothic in board and batten, and its posts are chamfered timbers with sawn brackets that answer to no order at all.
exceptions.bounds: There must be no classical capital anywhere on the building. The exception is for the ABSENCE of the order, not for its misuse.

confused_with.difference: That fault is between the column and what it carries. This one is inside the column.
That is a single ratio. This is a categorical mismatch of members, and a column can pass the ratio test and still be assembled from three orders.
